The refuter was right that step 5.1 claimed exact tooth-block sizes from a comb theorem that only gives a lower bound. The current proof now uses |B_i|>=|B|/ell^2, which is exactly what the ell>=y^{-1} estimate needs.

The refuter was right that the old proof chose a minimum over an arbitrary nonempty real set. The current proof replaces that with a finite minimum over the induced subgraphs of G and their actual sparsity thresholds.

The refuter was right that the reverse-direction P5 module check omitted several pair and triple cases. The current proof now lists all ten pairs and all ten triples explicitly before transferring primeness to the complement.

The refuter was right that the old diagonal language ignored the coded machines' input alphabets. The current refutation now diagonalizes on unary words 1^n against the filtered list of machines with s>=1, so every compared input is legal.
The refuter was right that the old p_m x_n argument forced the wrong value of |r|. The repaired proof now uses the unique doubled pair to force |r|=2m and then gets a direct length contradiction.

The refuter was right that the old statement treated a merely specified decoder as if it were machine-computable. The repaired theorem now states the computable input-decoder hypothesis explicitly and proves enumerability through binary code languages.

The refuter was right that the old proof had no licensed procedure for testing valid codes and reading back x from them. The current theorem now starts from a total enumerator and removes duplicate codewords directly.

The refuter was right that the old theorem overclaimed from an arbitrary chosen effective word encoding. The repaired theorem is narrowed to binary languages under the identity encoding, which is the version actually justified by the current proof.

The refuter was right that the displayed formula chi_{<=}(m,n)=chi_0(m dotted-minus (n+1)) recognized the wrong relation. The current proof now uses chi_0(m dotted-minus n), which is true exactly when m<=n.

The refuter was right that bare effective decodability does not yield a primitive-recursive decoder. The current proof now parses the explicit machine-code tuple with bounded arithmetic before doing the transition lookup.
The refuter was right that the old O(T(n)^2) statement dropped the input-length term from the standard simulator bound. The repaired theorem now states the correct O((n+T(n))^2) consequence.
The refuter was right that the old O(S(n)) statement ignored the simulator's stored input block. The repaired theorem now records the correct O(n+S(n)) space bound.

The refuter was right that the old theorem only translated valid codes and therefore did not define a decider on all binary inputs. The repaired statement now assumes polynomial-time/space validity tests and total translators on all binary words.

During the batch-9 risk review I found that the acceptance-class step cited the wrong fact: it needed the state-equivalence definition at the empty continuation, not the language-recognition definition from the start state. The current proof now cites and uses that empty-continuation argument explicitly.

During the batch-9 risk review I found that the old proof ran its machine on an abstract x in X rather than on an input code. The current proof now searches the enumerated codewords and halts exactly on the codes of elements of A.

During the batch-10 risk review I found that the proposition had become stale after the repaired fixed-machine simulation theorems: its proof still quoted O(T^2) and O(S) where the current theorems now require the extra n term. The current proof now uses O((n+p(n))^2) for time and O(n+s(n)) for space.
